_what: The studio's libraries. A `core` one is copied into every new game at creation under studio/; any other is an *extra*, copied only into a game whose template names it in `libraries` or whose person adds it. `npm run sweep` brings every existing game forward — core ones added, held ones raised, an extra never added; the version a game holds is recorded in its studio/studio.json. Bump `version` when the files change — the compatibility law (spec.md §4) says the new version must run every game the old one ran. `files` are the library's own, read-only to helpers; `vendored` names those among them that are somebody else's bytes — a font, an engine — which ride with a licence file beside them; `module: true` says the library is an ES module, loaded with <script type="module"> after every classic script, and a game using it has its own code as a module too; `seeds` are the game's own companion files, written once and never replaced. A seed's `from` is what an install with no choice at all writes: the input library's is the default control scheme, and templates/index.json is where a choice comes from.

input.what: One way in for the keyboard, a game controller and a touchscreen, for one player or two.
shape: - Every frame begins with Input.update(), before anything reads it, and the game asks Input.held,
Input.pressed and Input.axis rather than listening for keys itself. config/controls.js is where the
bindings live and where SCHEME says what a touchscreen gets. Read that word before writing any input
code: it was picked when the game was made and a person can change it in Controls whenever they
like, so it is a decision rather than a default — and the notes above it may still describe the
shape the game started as. Change it only if you are asked to, and then make the bindings match it.

sound.what: Plays the sounds in assets/sounds/ with one call — overlapping shots, loops, mute — and never breaks the game over a missing file.
shape: - A noise is Sound.play, by plain name, and it stays quiet about a file nobody has made yet — so the
call goes in before the sound does, in the same reply that asks for it.

sprites.what: Draws the pictures in assets/sprites/ by name, animated when the picture is a film strip of square frames, and never breaks the game over a missing one.
shape: - A picture is Sprites.draw, by plain name, and it stays quiet about a file nobody has made yet — so
the call goes in before the art does, in the same reply that asks for it.

screens.what: How big the game is on the screen, a phone-fit title and game-over screen, a HUD strip of score chips and meters, a one-line how-to-play hint worked out from config/controls.js and the device, and snippets to put inside a screen — the scoreboard above all, fetched and posted for you. A screen and a chip both take the game's own nodes. Carries its own two typefaces, so a game asks nothing of a font host.
shape: - It opens on a title screen rather than already running: Screens.title({ onStart: start }) puts up
the name, the tagline, one Start button and the how-to-play line, and calls start when pressed. A
tap on it reaches Input as one frame of "start", so a touchscreen needs nothing extra. A score is
what makes the same screen the game-over screen, so a run ends on Screens.title({ score, post: true,
board: true, onStart: start }). It returns { close } for taking it away yourself — there is no
Screens.close. Do not draw a title, a game-over banner or a play-again prompt of your own: those
three are the ones most often rebuilt by hand, and a hand-rolled one sits under the drawn touch
controls instead of stepping aside for them.
- How big the game is on the screen is Screens.fit(el), called once at boot with the canvas or the
box holding it — not width css of your own, which is the thing fit overrules. A game sized on the
window's width alone comes off the bottom of a phone held sideways, and every game here that was
written that way did.
- The numbers on screen while it runs are Screens.chips({ Score: 12, Lives: 3 }), a whole strip per
call and cheap to call every frame — not text the game draws for itself. A bar is a chip too:
{ Risk: { value: 43, max: 100, text: "43/100" } } draws a meter beside the number, and a node of
your own as a value puts anything else in the row, so there is no reason to build a HUD by hand.

moments.what: Lets the game say what just happened — a level gained, a run over, an ending reached — in one line, so achievements and the studio can listen.
shape: - Moments.say goes on the line where the thing happens, not in a batch at the end.

achievements.what: What a player can earn in this game, written in config/achievements.js as rules over the game's moments. Earned ones are kept forever by the studio and shown as a toast the moment they are won.
shape: - What a player can earn is a rule in config/achievements.js over a moment the game already says —
not a trophy list, a toast or a saved flag of the game's own. The library shows the toast and the
studio keeps what was won; Achievements.unlock is only for one no moment can describe.

physics.what: Things that fall, stack, roll, bounce and knock each other over — boxes and balls in the game's own pixels, built from a list in config/, on a steady clock so a tower falls the same way everywhere. planck.js underneath (Box2D, MIT).
shape: - A thing that falls, rolls or gets knocked is a body in Physics, built from a list in config/ with
Physics.build — not motion the game works out for itself. Physics.step(dt) once a frame, then draw
each body at its x, y and angle; Physics.onHit is where a crash becomes a sound and a moment. A
body's place in config/ is where it starts, so moving one is an edit there, never in js/.

render3d.what: A game drawn in 3D — boxes and balls in the game's colours, lit, with a camera that follows the player. three.js underneath (MIT). A module, so the game's own code that uses it is one too.
shape: - A 3D game is drawn by Render3D: studio/render3d.js is a <script type="module"> after every classic
script, and the game's own code that uses it is a module after that. Screens.fit(el) first, then
Render3D.start(canvas) — never a renderer, camera or light of the game's own. Many of the same box
(a floor, a maze) is one Render3D.boxes call, not a box each, or a phone cannot keep up. The world
is whole units with y up, and Render3D.draw(dt) is the last line of every frame.
